summary: Unit tests for two pure helpers: `iip/geo.py` (city-label normalization, great-circle distance and travel speed) and the incident-naming function from `iip/correlation.py`. Like `test_rules.py` they need no database, and they check the geographic maths against real-world distances, so the impossible-travel rule rests on verified numbers. The last test checks that a city name only counts when its country agrees.

notes.text: `datetime` and `timedelta` build the departure and arrival times for the travel test.
pytest supplies `parametrize` and `approx`, which compares floating-point numbers within a tolerance.
The geo module: `canonical`, `haversine_km`, `travel_between` and the `CITIES` coordinate table.
Only the pure naming function is imported. `correlate` itself needs a database, so it is exercised end-to-end by `test_simulation.py` instead.

Four label-normalization cases: a bare lowercase city gains its country; messy spacing and capitals are cleaned up; a city-state with no country part stays as it is; an unknown place is returned unchanged instead of being guessed.

Asserts that `geo.canonical` produces exactly the expected label. This matters because the risk engine compares labels (home city against event city), so dubai and Dubai, UAE must end up as the same string.

Checks the haversine (great-circle) formula against a known real distance: London to Paris is about 344 km. `pytest.approx(344, abs=5)` accepts anything within 5 km, allowing for rounding in the city coordinates.
A fixed departure time (midnight, 1 January 2026).
Computes a Dubai-to-London trip that takes exactly one hour.

The distance must be about 5,470 km (within 1%, via `rel=0.01`). Because the trip took exactly one hour, the speed in km/h must equal the distance, which proves the speed formula divides by hours correctly.
A trip to an unknown city, converted with `as_dict()` into the JSON-friendly form stored in an event's `context`.

With no coordinates there is no distance or speed, so both are `None`, not zero (zero would wrongly suggest a trip of no length). That `None` is what sends the rule engine to its time-window fallback.
Parametrizes the incident-title test over seven (signals, expected title) cases, one per line.

Failed logins plus privileged access is named Account takeover rather than Credential attack: `_PATTERNS` is ordered most specific first, so the two-signal pattern is checked before the single-signal one.
Rapid transactions gives Card testing; the extra Suspicious IP has no pattern of its own, so it doesn't change the title.
Single-signal patterns: Impossible travel keeps its own name, and failed logins on their own are a Credential attack.
Password spray wins. New device alone matches nothing, because the Unfamiliar sign-in pattern needs New device **and** Unusual location.
When no pattern matches, including an empty signal list, the title falls back to the default, Anomalous activity. `])` closes the list of cases.
The test itself runs once per case: it asserts `incident_title` returns the expected name. These titles appear in the incident queue, the incident detail and the AI analyst's answers.
The city fallback must respect the country.
"London, Ontario" is not London, UK: it stays an unknown place without coordinates (it used to make a Londoner in Canada look at home, and a Toronto trip look impossible).
A long country name still resolves, through `geo.COUNTRY_ALIASES`.
City-states have no country part, so any suffix naming the city itself is fine.
